Abstract
Recommender systems are central to debates over whether digital platforms fragment public discourse or sustain exposure to diverse information, yet empirical findings remain heterogeneous. This study examines how filter bubbles, echo chambers, and polarization are conceptualized and operationalized in recommender-system research and integrates evidence across algorithmic, behavioral, relational, and outcome levels. A systematic review of 60 studies published between 2020 and 2025, conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA, informs the development of the Platform-Mediated Polarization Framework (PMPF). Extending the recursive logic of Reinforcing Spirals Theory to computationally adaptive recommender environments, PMPF conceptualizes recursive exposure production as a process through which behavioral responses to prior exposure may be incorporated into subsequent ranking and personalization.
